content.title: About
content.content: Cucumber (Cucumis sativus) is an annual herbaceous plant of the gourd family, cultivated mainly as a vegetable. The edible fruit has a thin edible peel, juicy flesh, and a few small seeds. It is eaten raw, often used in salads, snacks, and drinks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cucumbers are about 95 % water, making them an excellent hydrating food.
The peel is rich in fiber and antioxidants, so it is often left on when eating.
There are over 100 cucumber varieties differing in shape, color, and flavor.
Cucumbers can be grown in greenhouses year‑round, but they prefer warm climates in nature.
In some cultures cucumbers are used in traditional medicine to soothe skin and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: Cucumbers are low in calories, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: Provide vitamin K, vitamin C, potassium, and magnesium, supporting bone and heart health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in the peel help combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Fiber in the peel promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cucumbers.

items.title: Pesticide Residues
items.content: Unwashed cucumbers may contain pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Digestive Issues
items.content: Large amounts can cause gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cucumbers are eaten raw in salads, as snacks, added to sandwiches, smoothies, and cold soups. The peel is usually left on, but can be peeled if desired. They can also be pickled to make dill or sour pickles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cucumbers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely wrapped in a perforated plastic bag. They keep for 5‑7 days when properly stored. Keep them away from ethylene‑producing fruits.
